Agreed to run benchmarks on Stratus sample prompts and share results; next meeting to scope a short pilot for on-prem private deployment.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we got about an hour, um quick intros?
[00:10] Priya (Stratus): Hi, I'm Priya, ML lead at Stratus, thanks.
[00:15] Tomás (SRE): Tomas here, SRE.
[00:18] Evan: Evan, infra.
[00:20] Alex: Great. Samir will kick into the technical part. Samir over to you.
[00:25] Samir (Redwood SE): Cool thanks. So today we wanted to focus on quantization for your inference workload — tradeoffs between INT8, FP8, GPTQ and AWQ, expected accuracy regressions, and how that interacts with KV cache and batching in our runtime. I'll start with a high-level summary then dig into benchmarks.
[00:45] Samir: Quick note, some transcriptions my be a bit rough, like we sometimes say K V cash for cache, but we'll clarify.
[00:55] Maya (Data Scientist): One thing up front — our main concern is that quantization doesn't break our hallucination filters; a 1-2% drop is okay but more than that becomes a problem.
[01:05] Samir: Totally. So historically INT8 gives good perf but sometimes bigger accuracy hits on certain heads. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quantization schemes that aim to reduce those regressions. GPTQ often retains more fidelity for generative tasks, AWQ is newer and can be better on some LLM architectures. FP8 is interesting since it keeps a wider dynamic range at lower precision but requires hardware support.
[01:30] Priya: Can you explain, like, what's the expected token latency improvement vs say, baseline FP16?
[01:38] Samir: Sure — roughly speaking, INT8 on commodity GPUs results in 1.6-2.2x throughput improvement and ~20-40% lower latency per token in our benchmarks, GPTQ tends to sit closer to INT8 in perf but with better accuracy retention for decoder-only models. AWQ can be competitive with GPTQ but results vary; on some models we saw AWQ matching GPTQ accuracy and giving slightly better speed. FP8 can be faster on hardware that natively supports it (like H100s with FP8 kernels), sometimes 2.5x throughput, but it's platform dependent.
[02:05] Evan: Are those numbers measured with KV cache warm or cold?
[02:10] Samir: Good question — the numbers I quoted are mixed; cold-start includes kv cache misses. With a warmed KV cache and our continuous batching, effective latency for many steady-state chats improves by another 10-20% since we avoid re-computing keys and values.
[02:25] Tomás: For our on-prem, we run A100s; no H100s yet. So FP8 isn't a practical option for us right now.
[02:32] Samir: Understood. For A100, INT8 / GPTQ / AWQ are the main paths.
[02:36] Priya: How do you evaluate accuracy regressions? We have a set of eval prompts and some business-critical outputs.
[02:43] Samir: We run a regen set — we do n-LLH comparisons, generation-quality metrics (ROUGE/BLEU in some cases), and a domain-specific scoring harness you can provide. For hallucination checks we do factuality prompts and also human-in-loop spot checks. We'll run the 1k prompt set you share through FP16, INT8, GPTQ and AWQ and calculate delta vs baseline.
[03:05] Maya: Sounds good. For GPTQ, I remember it can be slow to quantize — how long is that step?
[03:12] Samir: Yes, GPTQ requires a one-time offline pass — duration depends on model size: for a 7B model it's on the order of 30-90 minutes on a single A100; for 13B it's a few hours. AWQ and some INT8 workflows are faster, sometimes minutes to an hour. We can run quantization in our lab and share the artifacts, or provide the steps if you want to run in-house.
[03:32] Evan: On the security side, we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs for any artifacts you bring into our environment — how does Redwood handle key management for Private deployments?
[03:41] Alex: For Redwood Private we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, and HSM integrations in on-prem builds). We also produce audit logs and can retain them per your retention policy. We'll send the security checklist.
[03:53] Priya: Network-wise, we'll need to do VPC peering or private link; we also need options for an air-gapped variant.
[03:59] Samir: Our Private control plane can run within your VPC or on-prem. For air-gapped we provide an on-prem bundle; there are additional ops steps but we've done a few installs. We'll share the deployment doc and checklist.
[04:12] Priya: Are there any model-specific gotchas? We're currently using a customized Llama-derivative, about 13B with LoRA adapters.
[04:20] Samir: LoRA adapters complicate quantization slightly — if adapters are small and applied at runtime, quantization of the base model plus runtime application of LoRA is usually fine; however, if LoRA is merged before quantization, it changes the weight distributions and can affect GPTQ. We recommend quantizing the base then applying LoRA at inference or re-evaluating post-merge. We can test both workflows for your model.
[04:48] Maya: What about batching — we need low p99 latency for interactive chat, how do you balance batching and latency?
[04:55] Samir: Our runtime uses continuous batching with latency SLOs. We do dynamic batching windowing; for interactive paths we bias toward smaller windows and prefer KV cache and prefix caching to reduce compute per token. We can set per-route SLOs, e.g., 95th < 200ms, with batch size constraints. There's always a throughput vs latency tradeoff; we can tune it per endpoint.
[05:16] Priya: Any empirical numbers for p99 in an on-prem set up with INT8?
[05:21] Samir: From our tests on A100 clusters with warmed cache and small batch bias, we've seen p95 ~120-160ms token latency and p99 around 240-320ms for 13B models using INT8/GPTQ. But that depends on token length and concurrency.
[05:36] Tomás: Our concurrency patterns are spiky — lots of short bursts. Does Redwood support burst pools or reserved capacity?
[05:43] Alex: Yes Redwood Dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscaling policies. For Private we can help size the pool and provide recommendations for buffer capacity.
[05:50] Evan: Regarding KV cache persistence — can it be shared across nodes or is it local?
[05:55] Samir: KV cache is local to the runtime instance in the current architecture for maximal speed; we do prefix caching and can lease cold prefixes. For very large scale we offer distributed caching strategies but they add network overhead. Usually local cache with sticky routing works best.
[06:12] Priya: If cache is local, what happens when a request is routed to a different host?
[06:16] Samir: We do routing affinity; for sessions we try to keep the same instance. If fallback occurs, you'll get cold-start for that session until cache warms. We can also replicate hot prefixes for very high-value sessions.
[06:28] Maya: On accuracy — can you demonstrate a concrete case where GPTQ beats INT8?
[06:32] Samir: Yeah, we had a 13B decoder model where INT8 produced a ~3.5% drop on our domain QA benchmark, GPTQ reduced that to ~0.8%. AWQ was within 1.1% on that model. We'll include those benchmark specifics in the spreadsheet.
[06:49] Priya: Are there any licensing or IP issues with distributing GPTQ artifacts?
[06:53] Samir: No, GPTQ is a technique; artifact distribution depends on the model license — for some upstream models you may be restricted. We'll check license compatibility for your base model and include notes.
[07:05] Alex: Quick interjection — we also recommend a staged rollout: run GPTQ/AWQ in a shadow environment, run A/B or canary tests, compare latency and accuracy thresholds before pushing to prod.
[07:16] Priya: Makes sense. For the pilot, what's the minimal scope?
[07:19] Samir: Minimal pilot: you supply 1k prompts and the model (or we pull a matched open checkpoint), we run FP16 baseline then INT8, GPTQ, AWQ quantizations, run the eval harness, and provide delta metrics plus perf logs and kernel-level traces. We can run this within Redwood lab or on your infra if you prefer.
[07:39] Evan: If you run on-prem, how do we review kernel-level traces without exposing infra?
[07:44] Samir: We can redact IP and provide aggregated traces; or we run the quantizations and provide an artifact bundle that you can validate internally. For sensitive setups we hand off the steps so your team can run them and we help remotely.
[07:58] Tomás: About quantization artifacts — will the quantized model be a separate checkpoint file?
[08:02] Samir: Yes, usually GPTQ/AWQ outputs a quantized checkpoint that is separate. For some INT8 runtimes we use runtime quantization tables that sit alongside the checkpoint.
[08:12] Maya: Does Redwood runtime support AWQ out of the box?
[08:15] Samir: We have experimental AWQ support and it's in the verified model catalog for a few models; we can enable it for your pilot. It sometimes requires custom kernels.
[08:25] Priya: Any risks to downstream adapters and tokenizers?
[08:29] Samir: Tokenizer shouldn't change. Adapters — as I mentioned with LoRA, if you merge weights pre-quant you can shift distributions, so adapter strategy matters.
[08:38] Priya: What's the rollback path if accuracy regresses in prod?
[08:42] Alex: We support automatic fallback policies: traffic can be retargeted to FP16 baseline or to a different model variant if accuracy metrics cross thresholds. Rollouts can be canaryed.
[08:51] Priya: Okay. Anything else on the runtime side — memory footprints?
[08:55] Samir: Quantization reduces memory footprint significantly; INT8 can cut model memory to ~55-60% of FP16, GPTQ similar; AWQ varies. This impacts max batch sizes per GPU. We'll give you exact numbers for your 13B.
[09:09] Maya: For our LoRA adapters, is it cheaper to store them separately or merge them per quantized checkpoint?
[09:14] Samir: Storing separately is flexible and often preferred; merging simplifies runtime but may require re-quantization. We'll show cost tradeoffs.
[09:22] Priya: Can Redwood run the quantization step inside our VPC with our KMS?
[09:27] Samir: Yes, for Private deployments we can run work inside your VPC and use your KMS so artifacts never leave. For on-prem air-gapped we provide the tooling.
[09:36] Evan: What's the support SLA if we hit a perf regression in pilot?
[09:40] Alex: For Private customers we offer enterprise support tiers; for pilots we provide SE hours and a priority response window. We'll include the support options in the doc.
[09:50] Priya: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[09:54] Alex: Recap: Alex will send security docs and checklist; Samir will run bench comparisons and prepare the spreadsheet; Priya will share 1k prompts and model access; schedule a 2-hour pilot planning next week. Anything to add?
[10:08] Priya: No, that's good. Thanks everyone.
[10:11] Alex: Thanks all.
